passages.text: Traffic noise in cities is concentrated at low frequencies. Urban ecologist Priya Nair hypothesizes that, as a result, songbirds living in cities sing at a higher pitch than rural members of the same species, because higher notes are less likely to be drowned out by the rumble of traffic.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nair's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Within the same city, birds of one species that live near busy roads sing at a higher pitch than birds of that species living near quiet parks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Songbirds in cities begin singing earlier in the morning than songbirds in rural areas do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rural songbirds sing a greater variety of songs than city songbirds do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traffic noise in cities is loudest during weekday rush hours.

content.explanation: Nair's hypothesis links higher pitch to low-frequency traffic noise. If birds of the same species sing higher near busy roads than near quiet parks in the same city, pitch rises where traffic noise is greater, which directly supports the hypothesis.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is about the timing of songs, not their pitch.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is about the variety of songs, not their pitch.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This describes traffic noise but says nothing about how birds respond to it.

passages.text: Many farmers plant strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields. Entomologist Kofi Asante hypothesizes that these strips increase honey production, because honeybee colonies kept close to the strips have more flowers to feed on than colonies kept farther away.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Asante's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wildflower strips attract many butterfly species in addition to honeybees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Honey from farms with wildflower strips tends to be darker in color than honey from other farms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Honeybees often visit several different kinds of flowers during a single foraging trip.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within one farming region, colonies placed within 200 meters of wildflower strips produced about 30% more honey than colonies placed more than a kilometer away.

content.explanation: Asante's hypothesis is that being close to wildflower strips leads colonies to produce more honey. Choice D compares colonies in the same region that differ only in their distance from the strips and shows that the closer colonies produced more honey. That is exactly the pattern the hypothesis predicts.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This shows that the strips attract other insects, but it says nothing about how much honey bee colonies produce.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is about the color of the honey, not the amount produced.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This describes how bees forage in general; it doesn't connect wildflower strips to honey production.

passages.text: In recent years, a number of rural school districts have switched from a five-day to a four-day school week. Economist Lena Ortiz argues that most of these districts made the change mainly to save money on busing students, since rural buses must travel long distances each day.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ortiz's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students in four-day districts score about the same on state tests as students in nearby five-day districts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a survey of leaders of rural districts that adopted a four-day week, most named lower transportation costs as their main reason for the switch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many teachers in four-day districts say they prefer the new schedule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some districts that adopted a four-day week later returned to a five-day week.

content.explanation: Ortiz's argument is about why districts made the change: mainly to save on busing. Choice B reports that most leaders of districts that switched named lower transportation costs as their main reason, which directly supports her account of their motive.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is about the effect of the change on test scores, not the reason districts made the change.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Teachers' preferences don't show why the districts decided to switch.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This shows that some districts reversed the change, but it says nothing about why they adopted it.

passages.text: Psychologist Elena Varga is studying how toddlers learn new words. She hypothesizes that toddlers learn a word faster when an adult makes a gesture showing the word's meaning (for example, flapping arms while saying "flap") because the gesture gives the child extra information about what the word refers to.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Varga's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Toddlers who were taught words with meaningful gestures later used more gestures themselves when talking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Toddlers who were taught words with meaningful gestures remembered the words for longer than toddlers taught without gestures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Toddlers who were taught words with meaningful gestures learned them no faster than toddlers who heard the same words the same number of times without gestures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adults learning words in a foreign language also benefit from seeing gestures that show the words' meanings.

content.explanation: Varga predicts that meaningful gestures speed up word learning. Choice C describes a fair comparison (same words, same number of exposures) in which the gesture group learned no faster. If the gestures made no difference, the hypothesis that they help is weakened.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This shows a side effect of the gestures, but it says nothing about how fast the words were learned.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This suggests gestures help memory, which fits with the hypothesis rather than weakening it.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is about adults, and it points in the same direction as the hypothesis, so it doesn't weaken it.

passages.text: In a story, the narrator, Ines, keeps a detailed notebook about her grandmother's vegetable garden after her grandmother moves to another city. A critic argues that Ines's record keeping is less about the garden itself than about staying close to her absent grandmother.

content.stem: Which quotation from the story would most directly support the critic's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "The beans climbed the fence faster than I expected, nearly reaching the top by July."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "I bought a second notebook in August, because the first one had filled up."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "The neighbor's cat slept in the shade of the squash leaves most afternoons."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Each morning I wrote down which tomatoes had ripened, just as Abuela always had, and then I read the list aloud to the empty kitchen as if she might answer."

content.explanation: The critic claims the notebook is really a way for Ines to stay close to her grandmother. In choice D, Ines copies her grandmother's habit and reads the list aloud "as if she might answer," which shows that the record keeping is tied to her feelings about her grandmother, not just to the plants.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is a detail about the garden's growth; it doesn't connect the record keeping to the grandmother.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This shows Ines writes a lot, but not that the notebook is about her grandmother.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is a detail about the garden and a cat; it has nothing to do with the grandmother.

passages.text: Stalagmites grow upward from cave floors as water drips from the ceiling and leaves behind thin layers of minerals. Geologist Amara Okafor proposes that the stalagmites in one cave grew fastest during the region's wet periods, since more rainfall would mean more water dripping into the cave.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stalagmites in the cave are taller than those in several nearby caves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water dripping into the cave today contains dissolved minerals such as calcium.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mineral layers in the stalagmites that date to periods known from other records to be wet are thicker than the layers that date to dry periods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The temperature inside the cave has stayed nearly constant for thousands of years.

content.explanation: Okafor's proposal links fast growth to wet periods. Thicker layers mean more growth in a given time, so if the layers from known wet periods are thicker than those from dry periods (choice C), the stalagmites did grow faster when it was wetter.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Comparing heights with other caves doesn't show when the stalagmites in this cave grew fastest.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This explains where the minerals come from, but it doesn't link growth rate to wet or dry periods.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: A steady temperature says nothing about whether growth sped up during wet periods.

passages.text: After the premiere of his second symphony, composer Teodor Lisz revised the score. Musicologist Hana Brandt argues that the hall where the work premiered caused the revision: its sound made the brass instruments overpower the strings whenever the two groups played together, and Lisz changed the score to correct that imbalance.

content.stem: Which finding about the revised score, if true, would most directly support Brandt's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The revised score is about four minutes shorter than the original.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the revised score, the brass parts are marked to be played more softly only in passages where the strings are also playing; passages for brass alone are unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the revised score, the volume markings for every instrument are lowered throughout the symphony.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lisz also revised two of his other symphonies after their premieres, which took place in different halls.

content.explanation: Brandt's argument is specific: the problem was the brass covering the strings when both played together, and the revision fixed that. Choice B shows Lisz softened the brass only where they play alongside the strings and left solo brass passages alone, which is exactly the targeted change her argument predicts.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: A shorter score shows that Lisz made changes, but not that they addressed the balance between brass and strings.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Lowering every instrument's volume would not change the balance between brass and strings, so this doesn't point to the specific problem Brandt describes.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This suggests Lisz often revised after premieres, which if anything makes a habit, rather than this hall's sound, a possible explanation.

passages.text: The water in Lake Marren became noticeably clearer after 2015. Ecologist Jun Park claims that the change was caused by an invasive mussel species that reached the lake that year. Because these mussels filter tiny algae out of the water as they feed, Park argues, their arrival explains the lake's improved clarity.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Park's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of algae in Lake Marren's water decreased after 2015.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water clarity improved the most in the parts of Lake Marren where the invasive mussels are most densely packed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since arriving in Lake Marren, the invasive mussels have crowded out several native mussel species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Over the same period, water clarity improved by a similar amount in nearby lakes that the invasive mussels never reached, following a 2014 regional ban on fertilizer runoff.

content.explanation: Park says the mussels caused the clearer water. Choice D shows that lakes without the mussels became just as much clearer at the same time, after a regional change (the fertilizer ban) that could explain the improvement everywhere. If clarity improved by the same amount without mussels, the mussels are not needed to explain Lake Marren's change, which weakens Park's claim.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Less algae is what you would expect if the mussels were filtering it out, so this fits Park's claim; it is also consistent with other explanations, so it doesn't weaken the claim.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Clearer water where the mussels are densest supports Park's claim rather than weakening it.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This describes another effect of the mussels but says nothing about what caused the change in water clarity.

passages.text: Pots excavated from an ancient settlement are strikingly similar in shape and size. Archaeologist Rosa Mendel argues that they were made by specialists working in a single workshop rather than by individual households. Critics reply that the similarity alone is not decisive, since separate households following a shared tradition could also have produced very similar pots.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mendel's argument while addressing the critics' objection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pots from nearly every house in the settlement have the same shape and are almost exactly the same size.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pots of this style have been found in nearly every house in the settlement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The remains of pottery kilns were found in only one area of the settlement, surrounded by piles of broken pots that had cracked during firing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pots of a similar style have been found at another settlement about 50 kilometers away.

content.explanation: The critics accept that the pots are similar but say households could have made similar pots on their own. To answer them, Mendel needs evidence about where the pots were made. Choice C shows that pots were fired in only one place, which also holds the waste from making many pots. That points to a single production site rather than many households.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is just more evidence of similarity, which is the very evidence the critics say is not decisive.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Households all owning the pots fits either view: pots could be made at home or obtained from a workshop.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: A similar style at another settlement could reflect a shared tradition, which is the critics' alternative; it doesn't show where the pots were made.

passages.text: The striped reef goby, a small fish, can lighten or darken its body within minutes. Marine biologist Talia Moreno hypothesizes that the goby changes color to match its background, which makes it harder for predators to spot.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moreno's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gobies placed against a background matching their color were attacked by predators less often than gobies placed against a contrasting background.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gobies can change their color in less than two minutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Male gobies are usually slightly larger than female gobies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gobies are found on reefs in several different oceans.

content.explanation: Moreno's hypothesis says color matching protects the goby from predators. Choice A shows that gobies that matched their background were attacked less often than those that did not, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This shows how fast the color change happens, but not whether it helps the goby avoid predators.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is about the size of males and females, not color or predators.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is about where gobies live, not how color change affects predation.

passages.text: The silverleaf saltbush, a shrub that grows in dry scrublands, often loses most of its leaves in midsummer. Plant biologist Nadia Farouk hypothesizes that the shrub drops its leaves during droughts because doing so reduces the amount of water the plant loses through its leaves.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Farouk's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Silverleaf saltbushes grow faster in years with heavy rainfall than in dry years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The leaves of the silverleaf saltbush are covered in tiny silver hairs that reflect sunlight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When water was withheld from saltbushes for a month, the shrubs shed most of their leaves, and afterward they lost water much more slowly than they had before.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Animals in the region avoid eating saltbush leaves during droughts.

content.explanation: Farouk's hypothesis has two parts: the shrub drops its leaves when water is scarce, and dropping them reduces water loss. Choice C shows both. The shrubs shed their leaves when water was withheld, and then they lost water much more slowly. This directly supports the hypothesis.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is about how fast the shrub grows, not about whether dropping leaves reduces water loss.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This describes the leaves' appearance but says nothing about dropping leaves during drought or about water loss.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is about animals' eating habits, not about how the shrub's leaf drop affects its water loss.

passages.text: People who move to a new region often begin to talk like the locals, but not all features of speech may change at the same pace. Sociolinguist Owen Tallis hypothesizes that adults who move to a new region pick up local vocabulary much more quickly than they pick up local pronunciation.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tallis's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among adults who moved to a new city, most were using the local words for common objects within a year, but the way they pronounced vowels had barely changed after five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adults who moved from a nearby region sounded more like locals after five years than adults who moved from a distant region did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Longtime residents of a city could usually tell from a newcomer's accent that the person had grown up somewhere else.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children who moved to a new region adopted both local words and local pronunciation faster than adults who moved there.

content.explanation: Tallis's hypothesis compares two things for adult newcomers: how fast they adopt local words and how fast they adopt local pronunciation. Choice A gives exactly that comparison. The newcomers used local words within a year, but their vowel sounds had barely changed after five years, so vocabulary changed much faster than pronunciation.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This compares newcomers from nearby and distant places. It does not compare vocabulary with pronunciation.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This suggests newcomers keep their accents, but it says nothing about how fast they pick up local vocabulary, so it cannot show which changes faster.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This compares children with adults. The hypothesis is about adults, and the finding does not compare vocabulary with pronunciation.

passages.text: The number of households listed on the tax rolls of the medieval town of Wendmouth fell by about half between 1335 and 1350. Historian Lucia Ferrante attributes the decline to floods in 1338 and 1341 that buried much of the town's farmland in mud and sand, arguing that families left because they could no longer make a living from the land.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferrante's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Records from the period describe the flood of 1341 as more destructive than the flood of 1338.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Soil samples confirm that fields near Wendmouth were covered by a layer of flood sediment around 1340.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some families who left Wendmouth during this period resettled in villages on higher ground.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tax rolls from several nearby towns that sat on high ground and were never flooded show declines of similar size over the same years.

content.explanation: Ferrante argues that the floods caused Wendmouth's decline. If towns nearby that were never flooded lost a similar share of households over the same years, then something other than flooding (something that affected the whole region) likely caused the decline. Choice D therefore weakens her argument.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Comparing the two floods does not challenge the claim that the floods caused the decline. If anything, it fits her argument.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This confirms that the floods damaged the farmland, which supports Ferrante's argument rather than weakening it.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Families moving to higher ground fits the idea that they were escaping flooded land, so this supports her argument.

passages.text: In William Wordsworth's poem "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud" (1815 version), the speaker describes coming upon a great mass of daffodils beside a lake. A literary critic argues that the poem presents the experience as most valuable not in the moment itself but as a memory the speaker can return to long afterward.

content.stem: Which quotation from the poem would most directly support the critic's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude"

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way, / They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay"

choices.label: D
choices.text: "The waves beside them danced; but they / Out-did the sparkling waves in glee"

content.explanation: The critic claims the poem values the daffodils most as a memory the speaker returns to later. In choice B, the speaker is lying on his couch, often ("oft"), when the daffodils "flash upon that inward eye," meaning his memory or imagination, and this brings him "bliss." This shows the experience giving him joy long after it happened.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: These lines describe the daffodils as the speaker first saw them. They say nothing about remembering them later.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: These lines describe how many daffodils there were at the moment the speaker saw them, not his memory of them.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: These lines compare the daffodils with the waves during the original scene. They do not show the experience being valued as a memory.

passages.text: In many school cafeterias, students choose their own lunch items as they move along a serving line. School nutritionist Denise Okoro hypothesizes that students eat more vegetables when the vegetables are placed at the start of the line, where students see them first, instead of at the end.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okoro's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After one school moved its vegetables from the end of the serving line to the start, the amount of vegetables students ate rose by about a third, even though the menu stayed the same.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When surveyed, most students at one school said they would rather eat fruit than vegetables.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of the vegetables served in school cafeterias has risen over the past five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who bring their lunch from home eat more vegetables than students who buy lunch at school.

content.explanation: Okoro's hypothesis is that putting vegetables at the start of the line leads students to eat more of them. Choice A describes a school that made exactly that change with the same menu and saw vegetable eating rise by about a third, which directly supports the hypothesis.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is about students' preferences, not about where the vegetables are placed in the line.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The cost of vegetables has nothing to do with where they are placed or how much students eat.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This compares home lunches with school lunches and says nothing about the order of items in the serving line.

passages.text: The Ridgeback lizard lives at elevations from sea level to high in the mountains, and individuals at higher elevations tend to be darker. Ecologist Mateo Rivas claims that this dark coloring benefits lizards in cold mountain air because dark skin absorbs more sunlight, allowing the lizards to warm up faster.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Rivas's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At high elevations, a larger share of Ridgeback lizards are dark than at low elevations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ridgeback lizards spend more time basking in the sun at high elevations than at low elevations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At high elevations, dark Ridgeback lizards become active earlier in the morning than light ones do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When placed side by side in the same cold, sunny conditions, dark and light Ridgeback lizards warmed up at nearly identical rates.

content.explanation: Rivas's claim depends on the idea that dark lizards warm up faster than light ones. Choice D says that in the same cold, sunny conditions, dark and light lizards warmed at nearly the same rate. If that is true, dark coloring does not help the lizards warm faster, which weakens the claim.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This fits the pattern the text already describes and is consistent with dark coloring being helpful in the mountains, so it does not weaken the claim.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is about how long lizards bask at different elevations. It does not compare how fast dark and light lizards warm up.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Dark lizards becoming active earlier would suggest they warm up faster, which supports the claim rather than weakening it.

passages.text: Young male finches of a certain species learn their songs by listening to adult males. Neuroscientist Ingrid Haugen hypothesizes that what matters most for learning a song is when a young finch hears it, not how much of it the bird hears: in her view, song heard during a sensitive window early in life is learned well, while the same amount of song heard later is learned poorly.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haugen's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Young finches raised without hearing any adult song produced abnormal songs as adults.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among young finches that heard adult song during their first 60 days, those that heard more hours of it produced more accurate copies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young finches that heard 20 hours of adult song during their first 60 days copied it accurately, whereas finches that heard the same 20 hours of song only after day 90 copied it poorly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adult finches can learn to recognize the songs of new neighbors that move into their territory.

content.explanation: Haugen claims that timing matters more than amount. To support this, a finding must hold the amount of song the same while changing when it is heard. Choice C does this: both groups heard 20 hours of song, but only the birds that heard it early learned it well. The difference must come from timing, which directly supports her hypothesis.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This shows that hearing song matters, but it does not separate timing from amount, since these birds heard no song at any time.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This shows that the amount of song made a difference among birds of the same age, which points to amount mattering rather than timing.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Recognizing neighbors' songs is not the same as learning to sing a song, and this finding says nothing about young birds or a sensitive window.

passages.text: In a short story, Marcus, a retired lighthouse keeper, moves into an apartment in a busy city after forty years on a remote island. A critic argues that although Marcus insists he is glad to have left his old life behind, the story shows that he still arranges his days around the habits of his former job.

content.stem: Which quotation from the story would most directly support the critic's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Marcus told his daughter that the city's noise did not bother him; after forty years of wind, he said, a few car horns were nothing."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Each evening at exactly sunset, Marcus climbed to the roof of his building and stood there until the streetlights came on, as though checking that each one had been lit."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "'I don't miss it,' Marcus said when a neighbor asked about the lighthouse. 'Not for a minute.'"

choices.label: D
choices.text: "The apartment was small, but its kitchen window looked out over a park where children played until dark."

content.explanation: The critic claims that Marcus still organizes his days around his old job. A lighthouse keeper's work centers on lighting the lamp at dusk. In choice B, Marcus climbs to the roof "at exactly sunset" every evening and waits as though checking that the streetlights have been lit. This daily ritual mirrors his former duties, so it directly supports the claim.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This shows Marcus comparing the city to his old island, but it is about noise not bothering him, not about a habit from his job shaping his days.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This shows Marcus insisting he does not miss his old life, which is the part of the critic's claim the story undercuts. It does not show any habit from his former job.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This describes the apartment's view and says nothing about Marcus's habits.

passages.text: Rosalind Baptiste owns a small café. This spring she added an outdoor seating area, and over the summer the café's weekend sales rose sharply compared with the previous summer. Baptiste claims that the new outdoor seating is the main reason for the increase.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Baptiste's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Customers who sat outside ordered more desserts than customers who sat inside.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The outdoor seating area was full on most sunny weekends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other cafés in the neighborhood also added outdoor seating this year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weekend sales rose by the same amount on rainy weekends, when the outdoor seating area was closed, as on sunny weekends.

content.explanation: If the outdoor seating caused the increase, sales should have risen more when the outdoor area was open. Choice D says sales rose by the same amount even on rainy weekends, when the outdoor area was closed. That means something else must explain the increase, which weakens Baptiste's claim.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This suggests outdoor customers spent more, which if anything supports the claim.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: A full outdoor area suggests it brought in customers, which supports the claim rather than weakening it.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: What other cafés did does not tell us whether the outdoor seating explains this café's increase in sales.

passages.text: Dust blown onto glaciers can darken the ice, causing it to absorb more sunlight. Glaciologist Sigrid Olafsdottir hypothesizes, however, that dust speeds melting only when it forms a thin layer; a thick layer, she argues, acts like a blanket that shields the ice beneath it from the sun and actually slows melting.

content.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Olafsdottir's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ice beneath a dust layer a few millimeters thick melted faster than clean ice nearby, while ice beneath a layer several centimeters thick melted more slowly than the clean ice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: On average, dust-covered ice on the glacier melted faster over the summer than clean ice did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The amount of dust reaching the glacier each year has increased over the past several decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thickest dust layers on the glacier were found near its lower edge, where air temperatures are highest.

content.explanation: Olafsdottir's hypothesis has two parts: a thin dust layer speeds melting, and a thick layer slows it. Choice A supports both. Ice under a thin layer melted faster than clean ice, and ice under a thick layer melted more slowly than clean ice.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This shows that dust speeds melting on average, but it does not separate thin layers from thick ones, so it says nothing about thick layers slowing melting.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is about how much dust arrives each year, not about how the thickness of a dust layer affects melting.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This tells where thick dust layers are found but not how fast the ice under them melts compared with clean ice.
